newsitem.title: USA: Insurance chief executive pay up 13 percent in '95.
newsitem.headline: Insurance chief executive pay up 13 percent in '95.

text.p: Total compensation for chief executives at the 25 biggest U.S. insurance companies rose by a median 13 percent in 1995, about in line with the industry's return on equity, according to a new study.
The study, released on Sunday by management consulting firm Towers Perrin, found most of the growth in executive compensation for the year came in the variable, performance-based elements of pay.
The median increase in the CEO annual bonus was a sizable 22 percent in 1995, while the median increase in CEO base salary within the insurance industry was just 5 percent.

In dollar terms, CEO median total direct compensation -- salary plus annual bonus and the expected value of long-term incentives -- was just under the $3 million mark, considerably above the $2 million figure reported in 1994.

These increases came amid 13.7 percent average return on equity in 1995 and a median increase in earnings per share of 18 percent, reflecting an increasing linkage between senior management pay and corporate performance, the study said.

"Insurance companies have been revamping their executive compensation plans for several years -- and their efforts are showing in the growing linkage between senior management pay and corporate performance," said Richard Furniss, a New York-based executive compensation consultant for Towers Perrin.
"Perhaps most significant, short- and long-term incentives now collectively account for two-thirds of the average total CEO pay package," he said.
The study also revealed considerable variation in the pay practices among the companies in the survey sample.

Five chief executives received no salary increase, while one received a 22 percent raise, the study said. One chief executive received a bonus equal to four times salary, while two others received no bonus.
Insurance industry executives received a higher base salary in 1995 than their general industry colleagues.
The median base salary for insurance chief executives was $811,000, compared with $800,000 in general industry.
The median annual incentive award in the insurance industry was $775,000 for 1995, the study said. This represented 85 percent of salary, compared with 61 percent a year ago.
Stock options remain the most prevalent long-term compensation device used, with just under 88 percent of the companies granting options in 1995.
One-third provide restricted stock, while 44 percent use performance plans that pay out in cash or stock, the study said.

Cash compensation practices for outside directors in the insurance industry have remained fairly constant over the years. The median annual retainer and the median board meeting fees held at $25,000 and $1,000, respectively.
However, since the first analysis in 1989, the use of stock options or stock grants for directors has risen more than 12 times from 6 percent to 76 percent, the study said.
Deferred compensation arrangements have become far more prevalent as well, with 64 percent of the insurance companies reporting such plans in 1995, compared with just 17 percent in 1989.
